### What the forecast rests on {#sec-b1-sure}

```{python}
B1_PR = D.b1_prior_range()
B1_ALL = D.b1_all_range()
B1_COND = D.B1["conditional_on_parameters"][str(FINAL)]
B1_A2 = D.b1_sup("a2")
LM = D.B1_SUP["i_level_misses_points"]
B1_D2, B1_D4 = D.b1_run("S9"), D.b1_sup("g")
B1_S4_95 = D.b1_run("S4", stat="p95")
B1_T2 = D.b1_app_range([k for k in D.B1_APP_RUNS if k not in ("t1", "t3")])
assert B1_ALL[0] <= D.b1_app_range()[0] and D.b1_app_range()[1] <= B1_ALL[1]  # the prose: within that range
assert D.B1_APP["t1"]["convergence"]["gate_met_as_written"] and not D.B1_APP["t1"]["settings"]["rerun"]
# The test's realised share of floor years (section 4.3) is below the forward paths' and below 2001-25's (the prose says so).
assert REAL_FLOOR < min(B1_FWD_FLOOR[k]['floor_share'] for k in ('forward_2027_2038', 'history_2001_2025'))
assert B1_A2 > B1G["p50"] and B1_D4 < B1_D2 < B1G["p50"] and B1_D4 < B1_PR[0] <= B1_D2 <= B1_PR[1]
# Fat tails (S4) move the 95th percentile furthest among the prior runs (the prose says so).
_p95 = [D.b1_run(k, stat="p95") for k in D.B1_REG_PRIOR_RUNS] + [D.b1_sup(k, stat="p95") for k in D.B1_PRIOR_RUNS]
assert max(abs(v - B1G["p95"]) for v in _p95) == abs(B1_S4_95 - B1G["p95"])
```

The forecast is conditional on the model, its priors and the record, and five features of them move it or bear on how far it can be relied on. First, the record. Its forecast errors from `{python} V1_HOT` dominate it; @sec-b1 gives the median without them and at the outturns' scale. Changing one prior at a time, for the persistence, the tails, the correlation and the scales of shocks in both records, and removing the long-run shift or doubling its prior standard deviation, puts the median between `{python} bn(B1_PR[0], 1)` and `{python} bn(B1_PR[1], 1)`; quadrupling that standard deviation puts it at `{python} bn(B1_D4, 1)` (below). Every sensitivity run, listed in @tbl-b1-sens and @tbl-b1-sens-later, puts it between `{python} bn(B1_ALL[0], 1)` and `{python} bn(B1_ALL[1], 1)`. Among the prior changes, fatter tails move the `{python} V1_HI` percentile most, to `{python} bn(B1_S4_95, 1)`. Two refits specified after seeing every other run, one with the bound on $\Phi$ imposed by a change of variables and one with a fitted, persistent volatility in place of the Student-t shock, lie within that range (@sec-b1-appendix).

Second, the measure. The OBR forecasts calendar-year growth, while the rules use September CPI and May–July earnings, so the record's errors include how far the statutory inputs differ from calendar-year outturns. Fitting the model to calendar-basis errors lowers the median by `{python} bn(B1_BASIS[0], 1)`, and by `{python} bn(B1_BASIS[1], 1)` against a statutory fit on the same cells, so about that much of the median comes from that difference. Adding it back as a separately estimated term that does not persist from year to year gives `{python} bn(B1_A2, 1)`, above the headline, so the attribution depends on how that difference is modelled.

Third, the lower tail. The model's shocks are symmetric around a centre within about a point of the floor, so May–July earnings growth, the input that decides whether an April is earnings-led, falls below zero in `{python} pct(100 * B1_EARN_NEG, 1)` of forward path-years and below the record's lowest, `{python} rate(B1_EARN_MIN)` in May–July 2020, in `{python} pct(100 * B1_EARN_LOW, 1)`, against `{python} words(D.b1_below_zero('earnings')[1])` year below zero in `{python} words(B1_HIST_YEARS)` since 1989; September CPI falls below zero in `{python} pct(100 * B1_CPI_NEG, 1)`, against `{python} words(B1_CPI_NEG_HIST)` year, though CPI below the floor does not change the rule. Setting every negative input to zero leaves the median at `{python} bn(B1_CLIP["p50"], 1)` and lowers the `{python} V1_HI` percentile (@sec-b1). The upper tail and the mean therefore rest on inputs outside the record's range, so we report neither the mean nor the largest path saving. Compressing the lower side of every input towards a bound, at zero or just below the record's lowest input, lowers the median to between `{python} bn(B1_T2[0], 1)` and `{python} bn(B1_T2[1], 1)` (@sec-b1-appendix), so up to about `{python} bn(B1G["p50"] - B1_T2[0], 1)` of the headline median rests on shortfalls deeper than a bounded lower tail allows.

On the forward paths earnings growth is below `{python} FLOOR` in `{python} pct(100 * B1_FWD_FLOOR['forward_2027_2038']['floor_share'], 0)` of path-years, against `{python} pct(100 * B1_FWD_FLOOR['history_2001_2025']['floor_share'], 0)` of years over 2001–2025, the event that the baseline model overstated when it failed its test (@sec-paths-method); the centre's own earnings growth, `{python} pct(100 * min(B1_CENTRE_E), 1)` to `{python} pct(100 * max(B1_CENTRE_E), 1)` a year, is lower than the record's. The test's windows, which cover the inputs of `{python} FY_YEARS[0]` to `{python} FY_YEARS[-1]`, realised a smaller share than either (@sec-paths-method). Reweighting the forecast's paths to the share of 2001–2025 puts the median at `{python} bn(D.b1_tilt('years_2001_2025'), 1)`, and to the share in the test's windows at `{python} bn(D.b1_tilt('c2_test_windows'), 1)`; the reweighting also raises the paths' mean earnings growth, so it is a diagnostic, not a forecast (@sec-b1-appendix).

Fourth, the long run. The record's errors stop four years ahead, so years five to twelve rest on the fitted persistence and on priors for a long-run shift that no data here estimate. The record does show errors in the level that persisted: the statutory earnings input fell short of the spring forecasts made from June 2010 to March 2016 by `{python} num(-LM["origins_2010_2016"]["h3"]["earnings"], 1)` points on average three years ahead and `{python} num(-LM["origins_2010_2016"]["h4"]["earnings"], 1)` four years ahead, and exceeded those made from March 2017 to March 2022 by `{python} num(LM["origins_2017_2022"]["h4"]["earnings"], 1)` four years ahead. A wider long-run shift lowers the median, to `{python} bn(B1_D2, 1)` with its standard deviations doubled and `{python} bn(B1_D4, 1)` with them quadrupled.

Fifth, the parameters and the design. The median saving conditional on a single posterior draw of the parameters has a standard deviation of `{python} bn(B1_COND["gross_median_bn"]["sd"], 1)` across draws, and the share of paths above `{python} bn(TEN, 0)` runs from `{python} pct(100 * B1_COND["p_gross_above_10"]["p5"], 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * B1_COND["p_gross_above_10"]["p95"], 0)` between the `{python} V1_LO` and `{python} V1_HI` percentiles of draws. The Monte Carlo error of the median is `{python} bn(D.b1_se(FINAL, "gross_p50"), 2)`. With every forecast-error cell at full weight instead of the weighted likelihood the median is `{python} bn(D.b1_run("S14"), 1)` (@tbl-b1-sens).

We set the priors after seeing the whole record, and the prior on the shock scale is centred near the official one-year errors that the likelihood then fits, so those errors inform the forecast twice. The data move the shock scales and the tails; the posterior medians of each input's persistence and of the correlation stay close to their prior means (@tbl-b1-priors), so those priors carry through to the forecast. The priors alone, with no data, give a median saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` of `{python} bn(B1_PRIOR_PRED, 1)`, against `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 1)` with the data, a prior predictive check [@gabry2019].

Every sensitivity changes one feature at a time. None moves the prior means of the persistence or shifts the centre of the inputs, so forecast errors that persist with one sign are not covered: "as large as the record's errors" bears on their size, not their sign. Dropping `{python} V1_HOT`, fitting calendar-basis errors and bounding the lower tail each lower the median, and the three are not exclusive; we have not run them together. We designed the model after two others failed their tests; it is the seventh model set against the same short record, and we report its checks and apply no pass rule (@sec-b1-method).

### Robustness: four scenarios and stated volatility {#sec-budget}

@tbl-scenarios gives the reduction in State Pension spending under the adjusted Triple Lock, relative to the triple lock, on four scenarios, and @fig-scenarios the gross saving in each year. Two are single microsimulation runs. One is the OBR central path. The other, which we call the OBR long-term path, is our construction: it keeps the central path's inputs but pays the triple lock at the OBR's long-term triple-lock rate from April `{python} D.OBR_LT_FROM`, which phases in to earnings growth plus `{python} obr_premium` points, and applies the adjusted rule to the same inputs, so the premium goes to the triple lock only. The other two take `{python} N_DRAWS` simulated paths of prices and earnings, each run through the microsimulation under both rules, and move calendar-year earnings growth `{python} SHIFT` points a year lower or higher from `{python} FROM` (@sec-paths-method). We attach no probability to any of them, and the four do not form a probability interval.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scenarios
#| tbl-cap: "Reduction in State Pension spending on four scenarios, £bn, UK, cash. OBR paths are single microsimulation runs; earnings scenarios average `{python} N_DRAWS` simulated paths, ± the 95% Monte Carlo error. The last two rows reweight those paths to the realised share of floor years (@sec-scen-appendix). A scenario envelope, not a probability interval."
def _cell(v, e, d=1):
    return num(v, d) if e is None else f"{num(v, d)} ± {num(e, d)}"
NAMES = {"central": "OBR central path", "wedge": "OBR long-term path (triple lock at the OBR's long-term rate from April 2032)"}
body = []
for s in D.scenarios([MID, FINAL]):
    name = NAMES.get(s["key"], s["name"] + f", average of {N_DRAWS} paths")
    v = s["values"]
    sh, she = SHARE[s["key"]]
    g_cell = num(100 * GAP[s["key"]], 2) if s["key"] in ("central", "wedge") else \
        _cell(100 * SIM_G[s["key"]], 100 * SIM_GE[s["key"]], 2)
    body.append([name] + [c for y in (MID, FINAL) for c in (_cell(v[y][0], v[y][2]), _cell(v[y][1], v[y][3]))]
                + [_cell(sh, she, 2), g_cell])
for k, label in (("minus", f"Earnings {MINUS_SHIFT}, reweighted (diagnostic)"),
                 ("plus", f"Earnings +{SHIFT}, reweighted, mean earnings held (diagnostic)")):
    tr = TILT_ROWS[k]
    body.append([label, "–", "–", num(tr["share"] * BASE_SC[k], 1), "–", num(100 * tr["share"], 2),
                 num(100 * tr["G"], 2)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Scenario", f"{fy(MID)}: Gross", f"{fy(MID)}: Net", f"{fy(FINAL)}: Gross",
                           f"{fy(FINAL)}: Net", f"{fy(FINAL)}: Share of spending (%)", f"{fy(FINAL)}: G (log points)"],
                          body, "lrrrrrr")))
```

On the OBR long-term path the saving is `{python} bn(w_g, 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, `{python} bn(w_n, 1)` once income tax and benefits respond (@sec-net). Earnings lead CPI and the floor in every April from `{python} earn_from`, so the adjusted Triple Lock returns to its earnings path and then follows it, and the whole of the triple lock's excess counts as saving ($G_t = y_t$). The premium is the OBR's average allowance for years in which CPI or the floor beat earnings, which is an average over paths, not a path of CPI and earnings.

This scenario bounds the share of spending saved from above under the OBR's convention, and only under it: the expected share if the triple lock's expected excess equals the OBR's premium and the adjusted rule removes all of it. The scenarios and the forecast lie outside that convention, so they can save larger shares (@sec-b1 gives the forecast's excess and what its mean rests on). Since $G_t \le y_t$ on every path (@sec-formal), the expected gap under that convention cannot exceed the triple lock's cumulated excess on this path, from the floor-led Aprils and the premium together, `{python} points(WS["total"], 2)` log points; because $1 - e^{-G}$ is concave, Jensen's inequality gives the same for the share of spending, `{python} pct(SHARE['wedge'][0], 2)`. The argument reads the OBR's premium, an arithmetic allowance of `{python} obr_premium` points a year, as the expected log excess $\mathrm{E}[y_t]$ from the April `{python} SWITCH - 1` anchor. In cash the bound need not hold, because the triple lock's spending base rises with its excess, and the two co-vary across paths.

The two earnings scenarios give `{python} bn(lo_g, 1)` and `{python} bn(hi_g, 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. They are averages over paths from the model that failed the test, which the registered rule keeps as scenarios whatever the verdict. They are not a range around an unshifted case. Both lie between the forecast's median and its `{python} ordinal(75)` percentile; they are means over a failed model's paths and the forecast reports a median, so the comparison shows only that the two are of the same order. The adjusted rule's average gap is `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["minus"] / SIM_Y["minus"], 0)` and `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["plus"] / SIM_Y["plus"], 0)` of the triple lock's average excess (a ratio of averages). @sec-scen-appendix gives the arithmetic of the OBR long-term path, the scenarios' shares of spending, the split of their gap between the mean and the variation of their inputs, and a reweighting to the realised frequency of floor years, which lowers their gap.

In method, DWP's costing is closest to the OBR long-term path (@sec-dwp). In Great Britain our gross savings are `{python} bn(gb["central"], 1)` on the OBR central path, `{python} bn(gb["wedge"], 1)` on the OBR long-term path, and `{python} bn(gb["minus"], 1)` and `{python} bn(gb["plus"], 1)` on the two earnings scenarios. Scaled to DWP's spending base (@sec-dwp), the OBR long-term path's saving rises to `{python} bn(gb["wedge"] / sp_ratio, 1)` to `{python} bn(gb["wedge"] / flat_ratio, 1)`; allowing for DWP's rounding, that leaves `{python} bn(res_w_lo, 1)` to `{python} bn(res_w_hi, 1)` of DWP's figure that this path does not reproduce, `{python} pct(100 * res_w_lo / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * res_w_hi / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` of the £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn as published (`{python} pct(100 * res_lo / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * res_hi / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` on the scenarios).

Most of that residual is in the share of spending saved, not in the base: the Budget's chart (@sec-b1) saves a larger share of spending than the OBR long-term path, which saves `{python} pct(SHARE_MID['wedge'][0], 2)` in `{python} fy(MID)`, and in `{python} fy(FINAL)` a larger share than any of our scenarios (@tbl-scenarios). On the bound of @sec-formal, a saving of the chart's size in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, taken before rounding, corresponds to a triple-lock excess of at least `{python} points(CH_G, 2)` log points, about `{python} points(CH_PER, 2)` a year over the Aprils from `{python} CH_FIRST`, while the premium we apply phases in from April `{python} D.OBR_LT_FROM`.

Paying the premium in full from April `{python} SWITCH + 1` instead of phasing it in, and leaving every later April as on the path, in rule arithmetic with caseloads held, raises the gap on the OBR long-term path to `{python} points(WF['G'], 2)` log points, a share of `{python} pct(100 * WF_SHARE, 1)`, and the Great Britain saving at DWP's base to `{python} bn(wf_gb_lo, 1)` to `{python} bn(wf_gb_hi, 1)`, so an earlier start of the premium is large enough to account for much of the residual. It is one candidate among several: @sec-dwp lists the others, and we test none of them, nor do we know DWP's uprating path.

The OBR's own figures measure related but different things. Its replay of 1990–2025, with the anchor set in 1990, puts payments under the adjusted rule `{python} num(OBR_LO, 1)`% lower on average than under the triple lock and `{python} num(OBR_HI, 1)`% higher than under earnings uprating [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.51], so on that replay the adjusted rule removes about `{python} pct(100 * OBR_REPLAY_SHARE, 0)` of the triple lock's average log excess over earnings; the same average on our replay (@sec-past), over the Aprils from `{python} hw_first["first"]` to `{python} LAST_HIST`, is `{python} pct(avg_gap, 1)`. Its provisional long-term estimate, debt about `{python} num(DEBT_TL, 0)`% of GDP lower than under the triple lock and about `{python} num(DEBT_E, 0)`% higher than under earnings uprating in 2075-76 [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.52], corresponds to about `{python} pct(100 * OBR_DEBT_SHARE, 0)`. These are averages over years and shares of debt, not of the pension's level in one year, so they do not compare directly with the shares on our replay and our scenarios.

A further check gives the distribution of the saving if September CPI and May–July earnings growth vary around the OBR central path as they did over `{python} V1_SPAN`, with and without `{python} V1_HOT` (@sec-v1): a sensitivity conditional on stated volatility, on which no test bears. The forecast's median, `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 1)`, lies between its two medians.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "The saving grows through the decade on the simulated scenarios and the OBR long-term path, and stays small on the OBR central path. Gross saving, £bn, cash; bands are ± the 95% Monte Carlo error. Scenarios, not a probability interval."
F.scenario_years();
```

### The OBR central path {#sec-paths}

```{python}
crows = D.path_rows(central)
floor_years = [r["year"] for r in crows if r["tl_source"] == "floor"]
tie_c = [y for y in floor_years if y > D.last_price_led("central")]  # earnings rounds to the floor: neither leads
assert len(tie_c) == 1
after = [r for r in crows if r["year"] >= SWITCH]
first_earn = next(r for r in after if r["tl_source"] == "earnings")
differ = [r for r in crows if D.differs(r)]
p50, p90, rnd = D.path("monthly_p50"), D.path("monthly_p90"), D.path("random")
```

The OBR central path is one smooth path. The floor sets the triple lock in April `{python} listing(floor_years)` (in April `{python} tie_c[0]` May–July earnings growth rounds to the floor, so neither leads); from April `{python} first_earn["year"]` earnings lead every year (@fig-central). The two rules differ in `{python} words(len(differ))` year`{python} "" if len(differ) == 1 else "s"`, April `{python} listing([r["year"] for r in differ])`: after those Aprils the adjusted Triple Lock rises only by the floor, or by what brings it back to its earnings path, while the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level. By `{python} fy(FINAL)` the full new State Pension is `{python} gbp(52 * c_final["tl_weekly"])` a year under the triple lock and `{python} gbp(52 * c_final["bp_weekly"])` under the adjusted rule, and the saving is `{python} bn(c_g, 1)` (`{python} bn(c_n, 1)` net). The OBR finds the same for its forecast period: "`{python} obr_medium`" [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.50, footnote 17].

```{python}
#| label: fig-central
#| fig-cap: "On the OBR central path the floor sets the early rises, and the two rules differ in one April, 2032. Left: the inputs. Centre: each April's rise under each rule; the dotted line marks the switch. Right: the gap in the full new State Pension, %."
F.path_view("central");
```

### The mechanism on simulated paths {#sec-simpaths}

```{python}
SEL = {s["quantile"]: s for s in D.TRAJ["models"]["boot"]["selections"]}
QG = D.TRAJ["models"]["boot"]["gap_gbp_week"]
rnd_gap = D.row(rnd, FINAL)["tl_weekly"] - D.row(rnd, FINAL)["bp_weekly"]
rnd_q = max(int(k[1:]) for k, v in QG.items() if v <= rnd_gap)
rnd_q_hi = min(int(k[1:]) for k, v in QG.items() if v > rnd_gap)
LEADS = {pid: D.path_leads(pid) for pid in ("central", "wedge", "random", "monthly_p50", "monthly_p90")}
```

We run three simulated paths through the microsimulation: one drawn at random, and two picked near given percentiles of the gap between the rules in `{python} fy(FINAL)` among the baseline model's `{python} N_POP` draws, one at the `{python} ordinal(100 * SEL[0.5]["cdf_position"])` percentile and one at the `{python} ordinal(100 * SEL[0.9]["cdf_position"])`. The random path's gap, `{python} gbp(52 * rnd_gap)` a year, lies between the `{python} ordinal(rnd_q)` and `{python} ordinal(rnd_q_hi)` percentiles. Each is one path the model makes, not a forecast, and carries no probability weight. @fig-gaps shows how far apart the two rules end on each, beside the two OBR scenarios.

@tbl-paths gives each path's pension under each rule and its saving. The share of the triple lock's excess over earnings that the adjusted rule removes, $G_t/y_t$, is all of it on the two OBR paths, on which earnings lead in every April after the last price- or floor-led one in April `{python} D.last_price_led('central')`. It is less on the simulated paths whose last price- or floor-led April comes late, with too few earnings-led years after it to work off the excess by `{python} fy(FINAL)`: `{python} pct(100 * EXCESS['monthly_p50'][0] / EXCESS['monthly_p50'][1], 0)` on the path near the median gap, whose last such April is `{python} D.last_price_led('monthly_p50')`, and `{python} pct(100 * EXCESS['monthly_p90'][0] / EXCESS['monthly_p90'][1], 0)` on the path near the 90th percentile (`{python} D.last_price_led('monthly_p90')`). The random path's pension is higher under both rules because it draws higher CPI and earnings growth than the OBR's forecast, which also raises the spending base behind its saving. @sec-scen-appendix gives each path's changes of lead, floor years and Aprils with a rise below earnings (@tbl-path-features).

```{python}
#| label: fig-gaps
#| fig-cap: "On simulated paths the gap opens in a few steps and then persists. The adjusted rule's full new State Pension below the triple lock's, £ a year, on each path run through the microsimulation; single paths with no probability weight."
F.gaps();
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-paths
#| tbl-cap: "The paths run through the microsimulation, final year: full new State Pension under each rule (£ a year), gross and net saving (£bn), and the average loss among households with less income (£ a year)."
rows = []
for pid in ("central", "wedge", "random", "monthly_p50", "monthly_p90"):
    r = D.row(D.path(pid), FINAL)
    rows.append([cap1(PATH_NAMES[pid]), gbp(52 * r["tl_weekly"]), gbp(52 * r["bp_weekly"]),
                 num(r["gross"], 2), num(r["net"], 2), gbp(r["mean_loss"])])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Path", "Triple lock (£ a year)", "Adjusted (£ a year)", "Gross (£bn)", "Net (£bn)",
                           "Average loss (£ a year)"], rows, "lrrrrr")))
```

### From gross to net {#sec-net}

```{python}
acc = acc_w
dist = wedge["distribution"][str(FINAL)]
dec = dist["by_decile"]
hh = {r["hh_type"]: r for r in dist["by_hh_type"]}
pov = {p: wedge["poverty_pct"][p][str(FINAL)] for p in D.POLICIES}
low_dec = min(dec, key=lambda d: d["pct_income_change"])
EXP = "monthly_p50"  # the example pensioners' path: the OBR long-term run carries no example households
_shares = [D.borne_share(e, FINAL) for e in D.examples(D.path(EXP)).values()]
ex_lo = min(x for x in _shares if x is not None and x > 0.005)
ex_hi = max(x for x in _shares if x is not None)
ex_gain = sum(x is not None and x < -0.005 for x in _shares)
```

@tbl-account follows the gross saving on the OBR long-term path to the net saving. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` extra Pension Credit offsets `{python} bn(-acc["rows"][0][1])` of the `{python} bn(acc["gross"])` gross saving and lower income tax `{python} bn(-acc["rows"][5][1])`, leaving `{python} bn(acc["net"])` net, `{python} pct(100 * acc["net"] / acc["gross"], 0)` of the gross. The net figure counts direct taxes and benefits only, with no change in behaviour. It leaves out VAT and other indirect taxes on pensioners' lower spending, which would make it smaller. Some offsets fall on other budgets: local authorities pay council tax reduction in Great Britain, and part of the income tax would otherwise go to the Scottish and Welsh governments.

@tbl-account bounds the Pension Credit convention of @sec-model in one direction only. If the Pension Credit guarantee followed each rule's rise, the Pension Credit, Housing Benefit and council tax reduction offsets, `{python} bn(pc_hb_ctr, 2)` together, would vanish and could change sign, because a lower Pension Credit guarantee also lowers awards to existing claimants and moves fewer people onto the guarantee credit. The net saving on this path would then be at least about `{python} bn(pc_lb, 1)`, `{python} pct(100 * pc_lb / acc["gross"], 0)` of the gross; we do not estimate how far above. Applied to the forecast's median gross saving, that ratio gives at least about `{python} bn(B1G["p50"] * pc_lb / acc_w["gross"], 1)`, a single path's ratio, not a forecast of its own.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-account
#| tbl-cap: "From gross to net on the OBR long-term path in the final year, £ billion. Offsets are signed to sum to the net saving; figures may not sum because of rounding."
# Universal Credit barely moves for pensioners; it is folded into the other taxes and benefits.
small = [(label, v) for label, v in acc["rows"] if "Universal Credit" in label]
body = [["Gross saving (State Pension)", num(acc["gross"], 2)]]
body += [[label, num(v, 2)] for label, v in acc["rows"] if (label, v) not in small]
body.append(["Other taxes and benefits", num(acc["other"] + sum(v for _, v in small), 2)])
body.append(["**Net saving**", f'**{num(acc["net"], 2)}**'])
display(Markdown(md_table(["", f"{fy(FINAL)} (£bn)"], body)))
```

### Who has less income {#sec-incomes}

The household results come from the same runs. The model recalculates every pensioner's State Pension and, with it, their income tax, Pension Credit, Housing Benefit, council tax reduction and Winter Fuel Payment. We report them on the OBR long-term path, the larger of the two OBR runs, and give the poverty changes on the OBR central path and the two simulated paths picked by their gap beside it. Cash and percentage changes in income scale roughly with the gap in the pension; poverty rates do not.

On the OBR long-term path households with less income under the adjusted Triple Lock than under the triple lock in `{python} fy(FINAL)` have `{python} gbp(w_loss)` a year less on average, against `{python} gbp(c_final["mean_loss"])` on the OBR central path. Single pensioners have `{python} pct(-hh["single_pensioner"]["pct_income_change"], 1)` less income than under the triple lock on average, and pensioner couples `{python} pct(-hh["pensioner_couple"]["pct_income_change"], 1)`. The share of households with at least £1 a year less income, `{python} ("about " + pct(lose_hi, 0)) if pct(lose_lo, 0) == pct(lose_hi, 0) else (pct(lose_lo, 0) + " to " + pct(lose_hi, 0))` on every path, counts the households that receive a State Pension and says nothing about the size of the effect.

@fig-deciles ranks households by equivalised household net income before housing costs under the triple lock, with each decile holding a tenth of people, and gives each decile's total change in income as a share of its total income. Relative to income, the change is largest in the `{python} ordinal(low_dec["decile"])` decile, at `{python} pct(abs(low_dec["pct_income_change"]), 2)` of income, and smaller in the lowest-income and in the higher-income deciles. The guarantee credit, which makes up a lower pension pound for pound for those who claim it, and the State Pension's smaller share of higher incomes both work in this direction. Four example pensioners in @sec-examples show the range: on the model path near the median gap, the share of the lower pension that reaches their income in `{python} fy(FINAL)` runs from `{python} pct(100 * ex_lo, 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * ex_hi, 0)` for those whose income falls, and `{python} words(ex_gain)` ends with a higher income because of a threshold.

On the OBR central path, where the pension gap is small, no poverty measure changes by more than `{python} num(pov_c_max, 2)` percentage points. On the OBR long-term path pensioner poverty after housing costs is `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_absolute_ahc"], 2)` points higher against the fixed line and `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_relative_ahc"], 2)` points higher against the relative one, and on the simulated path near the 90th percentile of the gap up to `{python} num(pov_p90_max, 2)` points higher (@tbl-poverty). Pensioners here are people over State Pension age.

The poverty changes on single paths carry no sampling margin, and we have not benchmarked the model's levels: pensioner relative poverty after housing costs under the triple lock is `{python} pct(wedge["poverty_pct"]["triple_lock"][str(D.YEARS[0])]["pensioners_relative_ahc"], 1)` in `{python} fy(D.YEARS[0])`, the first year of the runs, against about `{python} dwp_pov.group(1)` in DWP's modelling for `{python} fy(int(dwp_pov.group(2)[:4]))`, also for people above State Pension age [@dwp_uprating2026]; Households Below Average Income statistics instead count people in pensioner families.

Poverty among everyone changes much less, and relative poverty among everyone falls: the relative line is 60% of median income in each run, and the lower pension lowers the median, so fewer people of working age fall below the line. The fixed line, uprated with each path's CPI, differs between paths and from the official absolute measure, which DWP anchors in 2010-11.

Pension Credit makes up much of a lower pension for pensioners on the guarantee credit, but not for those just above it, nor for those entitled who do not claim. These household results hold the Pension Credit guarantee to earnings under both rules; if it instead followed each rule's rise, it would be lower under the adjusted rule, so the losses of Pension Credit recipients and the poverty changes would be larger, and we do not estimate them. DWP also projects pensioner relative poverty after housing costs under the adjusted Triple Lock falling from around `{python} dwp_pov.group(1)` to around `{python} dwp_pov.group(3)` by `{python} dwp_pov.group(4)`-`{python} dwp_pov.group(5)[-2:]`, against a poverty line projected forward with earnings; our changes compare the adjusted Triple Lock with the triple lock in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, with a line set each year from the simulated incomes, so they answer a different question.

```{python}
F.deciles("wedge");
```

Fixed line: 60% of the 2024-25 median uprated by each path's CPI. Relative: 60% of the median in the same run. Single runs, Pension Credit guarantee linked to earnings under both rules."
```{python}
PM = [("pensioners_absolute_ahc", "Pensioners, fixed line"), ("pensioners_relative_ahc", "Pensioners, relative"),
```

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

The adjusted Triple Lock still raises the pension each year by at least CPI and the `{python} FLOOR` floor, but lets the pension fall back to its April `{python} SWITCH - 1` value relative to earnings after years in which prices or the floor beat earnings. For the UK in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, a Bayesian forecast of the uprating inputs puts the median reduction in State Pension spending at about `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 0)`, with half of paths between `{python} bn(B1G["p25"], 1)` and `{python} bn(B1G["p75"], 1)`, conditional on the model, on priors set after seeing the record and on forecast errors over `{python} B1_FWD_SPAN` as large as those one to four years ahead over `{python} B1_ERR_SPAN`, extended by the model; without `{python} V1_HOT` in the record the median is `{python} bn(B1_S7, 1)`, and with errors the size of past outturn variation `{python} bn(B1_S12, 1)`.

After income tax and benefits respond, the median is `{python} bn(B1N["p50"], 1)` with the Pension Credit guarantee linked to earnings under both rules, and, applying the OBR long-term path's ratio of net to gross under the other convention, at least about `{python} bn(B1G["p50"] * pc_lb / acc_w["gross"], 1)` if it followed each rule's rise (@sec-net). On the OBR's central path the rule saves `{python} bn(c_g, 1)`, and the scenarios with earnings growth `{python} SHIFT` points lower or higher give `{python} bn(lo_g, 1)` and `{python} bn(hi_g, 1)`; on a single path through each scenario's mean inputs the gap is much smaller, so most of the saving comes from year-to-year variation in the inputs (@sec-scen-appendix). Scaled to DWP's spending base, our closest scenario leaves `{python} pct(100 * res_w_lo / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * res_w_hi / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` of DWP's £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn unreproduced. In rule arithmetic with caseloads held, paying the OBR's premium in full from April `{python} SWITCH + 1` would be large enough to account for much of that residual, but we do not know DWP's uprating path and have not tested the other candidate sources (@sec-dwp).

The reduction in spending is lower income for the households that receive a State Pension, with Pension Credit and income tax making up part of it. On the OBR long-term path, whose gross saving is `{python} bn(w_g, 1)`, those that lose have `{python} gbp(w_loss)` a year less on average, about `{python} gbp(round(w_loss * B1G["p50"] / w_g, -1))` scaled to the forecast's median saving. Pensioner poverty after housing costs rises by `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_absolute_ahc"], 2)` percentage points against the fixed line and `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_relative_ahc"], 2)` against the relative one, in a single run whose poverty levels we have not benchmarked (@sec-incomes). Both results hold the Pension Credit guarantee linked to earnings; if it instead followed each rule's rise, the losses of Pension Credit recipients and the poverty changes would be larger, which we do not estimate.

For any rule that takes the highest of several indices, the saving from an earnings anchor depends on how the indices vary, not only on their averages. The anchor removes all of the excess on the OBR's two smooth paths, where earnings lead in every April after the floor-led ones, `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)` of it on the replay from April `{python} hw_first["first"]`, and about a third on the forecast's paths by `{python} fy(FINAL)`, a share still rising at the end of the horizon. On those paths the centre sits close to the floor in the first Aprils, so price- or floor-led years are common, and afterwards it gives earnings only a small average lead relative to the year-to-year variation, so within ten years the earnings-led years work off only part of the excess.

The analysis has limits. The forecast's probabilities hold under its model and priors, which we set after seeing the whole record and two failed models; it departs from the second model's registered scenarios-only fallback by our decision, not because it passed a test (@sec-b1-method). As first coded it exceeded its convergence gate's limit twice; the headline's fit, sampled without the wall under the plan's clause for coding errors, meets the gate's limits, and a later refit with the bound imposed by a change of variables meets the gate as written and gives the same median.

Its symmetric shocks give nominal earnings falls in `{python} pct(100 * B1_EARN_NEG, 0)` of path-years, far more often than the record, and bounding that tail lowers the median by up to `{python} bn(B1G["p50"] - B1_T2[0], 1)`; no run combines that with dropping `{python} V1_HOT` or the calendar basis, each of which lowers it by a similar amount. On one way of modelling it, about `{python} bn(B1_BASIS[0], 1)` of the median comes from how the statutory inputs differ from calendar-year outturns, and beyond four years ahead the forecast rests on fitted persistence and priors, whose means the data barely move.

We measure cash flows only and do not value the insurance against price- or floor-led years that pensioners lose under the adjusted rule. Our runs hold behaviour fixed and leave out indirect taxes, and the forecast converts every path to cash at the central run's population and entitlements. The survey is aged to `{python} fy(FINAL)` statically, reweighted on age and sex only, with entitlements carried forward from today's pensioners, so every cash figure scales with a spending base that is below DWP's (@sec-dwp). Letting deaths and later cohorts' entitlements differ, as DWP's projection does, needs new microsimulation runs. Outcomes not yet observed are the only clean test of any of these distributions (@sec-test).

## Appendix: proofs {#sec-proof .appendix}

*The recursions.* From the level equations, $y_t - y_{t-1} = \ln(1 + \max(m_t, e_t)) - \ln(1 + e_t) = \max(d_t, 0)$, and $x_t = \ln \max\bigl((L_{t-1}/A_{t-1})(1 + m_t)/(1 + e_t),\, 1\bigr) = \max(x_{t-1} + d_t, 0)$. Hence $\Delta G_t = \max(d_t, 0) - \max(d_t, -x_{t-1})$, which is zero when $d_t \ge 0$ and $\min(-d_t, x_{t-1})$ when $d_t < 0$; since $x_{t-1} \ge 0$ this is $\min(\max(-d_t, 0), x_{t-1}) \ge 0$. Summing, the reflected walk has the standard solution of a Lindley recursion, $x_t = D_t - \min_{T_0 \le s \le t} D_s$ [@asmussen2003], and $y_t = \sum_s \max(d_s, 0)$, which gives the closed form for $G_t$. The upper bounds follow from $x_t \ge 0$ and from $\min_s D_s \le D_{T_0} = 0$.

*Proposition 1.* If $\Delta G_r > 0$ then $d_r < 0$ and $x_{r-1} > 0$, and $x_{r-1} > 0$ requires some $s < r$ with $d_s > 0$, since $x$ starts at zero and rises only when $d > 0$. Conversely, take $s$ with $d_s > 0$ and the first $r > s$ with $d_r < 0$; between them every $d \ge 0$, so $x_{r-1} \ge x_s \ge d_s > 0$ and $\Delta G_r > 0$. So $G_t > 0$ exactly when such a pair $s < r \le t$ exists. If $d_s \le 0$ in every year, $x$ stays at zero and $G_t = y_t = 0$; if $d_s \ge 0$ in every year, no increment is positive and $G_t = 0$.

*Proposition 2.* Write $n$ for the number of rises and number the differences $d_1, \dots, d_n$, with $S_k = d_1 + \dots + d_k$ and $S_0 = 0$. The solution of the Lindley recursion is $x_n = S_n - \min_{0 \le s \le n} S_s = \max_{0 \le s \le n} (S_n - S_s)$, and $S_n - S_s$ is the sum of the last $n - s$ differences. Under independence with a common distribution, $(d_1, \dots, d_n)$ has the same law as $(d_n, \dots, d_1)$, so $x_n$ has the law of the running maximum $\max_{0 \le k \le n} S_k$, whose expectation is $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathrm{E}[(S_k)^{+}]/k$ by Spitzer's identity [@spitzer1956]. With $\mathrm{E}[y_n] = n\,\mathrm{E}[d^{+}]$ this gives the expression for $\mathrm{E}[G_n]$. If $d \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ then $S_k \sim N(k\mu, k\sigma^2)$, and for $X \sim N(m, s^2)$, $\mathrm{E}[X^{+}] = m\,F(m/s) + s\,f(m/s)$, with $F$ and $f$ the standard normal distribution and density functions, whose derivative in $s$ is $f(m/s)$. Hence
$$\frac{\partial\, \mathrm{E}[G_n]}{\partial \sigma} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \Bigl(f(\mu/\sigma) - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\,f(\sqrt{k}\,\mu/\sigma)\Bigr) \ge 0,$$
since $f(\sqrt{k}\,a) \le f(a)$ and $1/\sqrt{k} \le 1$ for $k \ge 1$. At $\sigma = 0$ each term of $\mathrm{E}[G_n]$ is $\mu^{+} - (k\mu)^{+}/k = 0$.

*Proposition 2 on the replay and the scenarios.* At the mean and standard deviation of $d_t$ on the replay's inputs from April `{python} hw_first["first"]` to April `{python} LAST_HIST` (`{python} points(H_MU, 2)` and `{python} points(H_SD, 2)` log points) Proposition 2 gives an expected gap of `{python} points(SP_H[0], 2)` log points over those `{python} words(len(HD))` Aprils and an expected excess of `{python} points(SP_H[1], 2)`, against `{python} points(G_HIST, 2)` and `{python} points(Y_HIST, 2)` on the replay itself (@sec-past). At the pooled mean and standard deviation of $d_t$ on each earnings scenario's paths from April `{python} SWITCH` it gives `{python} points(SP_S["minus"][0], 2)` and `{python} points(SP_S["plus"][0], 2)` log points by `{python} fy(FINAL)`, against path averages of `{python} points(SIM_G["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_G["plus"], 2)` (@tbl-scenarios), and expected excesses of `{python} points(SP_S["minus"][1], 2)` and `{python} points(SP_S["plus"][1], 2)` against `{python} points(SIM_Y["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_Y["plus"], 2)`.

## Appendix: model details and the data against DWP's forecasts {#sec-appendix .appendix}

This appendix gives details of the model that @sec-method summarises, sets the data against DWP's forecasts and reconciles our figures with DWP's costing.

PolicyEngine UK's behavioural responses each compare a simulation with a baseline. PolicyEngine UK builds a baseline for every simulation; our code removes it, so no response runs and behaviour stays fixed in every run. The step on the OBR's labour-supply elasticities changes the earnings of employees only, for the two eldest adults in each household, with its participation response disabled, and it leaves out people aged `{python} V2["lsr_excluded_from_age"]` and over, the self-employed and full-time students. A second labour-supply response, whose elasticities are zero unless a user sets them, has no age limit; like the response of capital gains realisations to tax rates, it is zero without a baseline. The State Pension is not withdrawn as earnings rise, so a lower pension would change the work incentives of younger household members mainly through an income effect, which we do not model.

For later years PolicyEngine UK would scale every household weight by the ONS's growth in the total population. Our code replaces that step. In each year after `{python} V2["anchor_year"]` it rakes the `{python} V2["anchor_year"]` household weights, by a bounded calibration that minimises their relative entropy and keeps each weight between `{python} num(D.RAKE_BOUNDS[0], 1)` and `{python} num(D.RAKE_BOUNDS[1], 0)` times its `{python} V2["anchor_year"]` value. The weighted number of people in each of `{python} count(D.RAKE_CELLS)` age and sex cells (five-year bands under `{python} D.RAKE_SINGLE[0]`, single years from `{python} D.RAKE_SINGLE[0]` to `{python} D.RAKE_SINGLE[1]`, then `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[0][0]` to `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[0][1] - 1`, `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[1][0]` to `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[1][1] - 1` and `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[2][0]` and over) then grows from its `{python} V2["anchor_year"]` level as in the ONS's 2024-based population projection, with each fiscal year taking three quarters of the mid-year population of its first year and a quarter of the next (@sec-population).

In each April since 2022 the Pension Credit guarantee has risen by the same percentage as the State Pension, as in April 2023, when both rose by `{python} rate(hist_gc[0])` against earnings growth of `{python} rate(hist_gc[1])` [@uprating2023]; in every earlier April from 2013 in which prices or the floor set the State Pension's rise it rose by less, by the basic State Pension's cash increase in April 2013, 2014, 2015, 2018 and 2021 and by about earnings growth in April 2017 [@uprating2013; @uprating2014; @uprating2015; @uprating2017; @uprating2018; @uprating2021].

@tbl-coverage sets the data against DWP's benefit expenditure and caseload forecasts [@dwp_bect2026].

```{python}
#| label: tbl-coverage
#| tbl-cap: "Our data against DWP's Spring Forecast 2026, Great Britain. Microcosm underlies every result; the Enhanced FRS is a check. Claims count benefit units. (a) DWP includes payments abroad. (b) Excludes Universal Credit housing costs."
COV_LABELS = {
    "state_pension_bn": "State Pension, excluding payments abroad (£bn)",
    "flat_rate_bn": "Basic and new State Pension (a) (£bn)",
    "state_pension_recipients_m": "State Pension recipients (m)",
    "pension_credit_bn": "Pension Credit (£bn)",
    "pension_credit_claims_m": "Pension Credit claims (m)",
    "housing_benefit_bn": "Housing Benefit, all ages (b) (£bn)",
    "housing_benefit_pension_age_bn": "Housing Benefit, pension age (£bn)",
    "housing_benefit_pension_age_claims_m": "Housing Benefit claims, pension age (m)",
}
body = []
for r in cov["rows"]:
    d = 2 if r["key"].endswith("_m") else 1
    body.append([COV_LABELS.get(r["key"], r["label"]), num(r["dwp"], d),
                 num(r["primary_gb"], d), pct(100 * r["primary_gb_over_dwp"], 0),
                 num(r["sensitivity_gb"], d), pct(100 * r["sensitivity_gb_over_dwp"], 0)])
display(Markdown(md_table([fy(cov["year"]), "DWP", "Microcosm: Value", "Microcosm: % of DWP",
```

### The reconciliation with DWP's costing {#sec-dwp}

DWP's method note says that "`{python} dwp_model`" and that "`{python} dwp_cpi`" [@dwp_uprating2026]; its model is a dynamic microsimulation model of the kind @li2013 review. The Government has said, in answer to a parliamentary question, that DWP's analysis did not use single-year earnings or prices growth assumptions [@hl3774]. That makes it closer in kind to the OBR's average-rate convention than to a simulated path, so we infer that the OBR long-term path is the closest of our scenarios in method.

The population also differs. DWP projects deaths, migration and State Pension entitlements, while we keep today's survey records and rake their weights to the ONS's projected growth by age and sex (@sec-population). Our survey's spending on the basic and new State Pension, the base the saving scales with, is `{python} pct(100 * flat_ratio, 0)` of DWP's forecast for `{python} fy(cov["year"])` (@tbl-coverage), but that ratio compares our Great Britain base with a DWP base that includes State Pensions paid abroad, which DWP's Great Britain costing leaves out. On total State Pension excluding payments abroad our survey matches `{python} pct(100 * sp_ratio, 0)` of DWP's forecast, so the like-for-like ratio for the basic and new State Pension lies between `{python} num(flat_ratio, 2)` and about `{python} num(sp_ratio, 2)`. Since the gross saving is close to $(1 - e^{-G_t})B^{\mathrm{TL}}_t$, scaling our base to DWP's raises the Great Britain figures in proportion (@sec-budget).

Besides the start date of the OBR's premium (@sec-budget), candidate sources of the residual, none of which we test, are DWP's own uprating path, later cohorts' larger new State Pension entitlements, which our base may understate (`{python} pct(100 * new_sp_share, 0)` of recipients in `{python} fy(FINAL)` in the raked survey are on the new State Pension, with entitlements carried forward from today's pensioners), and State Pension age. Both of the Budget chart's lines fall as a share of GDP from `{python} fy(CH_DIPS[1][0])` to `{python} fy(CH_DIPS[1][1])`, as they do from `{python} fy(CH_DIPS[0][0])` to `{python} fy(CH_DIPS[0][1])` while State Pension age rises to `{python} SPA_67`; our runs keep State Pension age on the law's timetable, which reaches `{python} SPA_68` only from `{python} SPA_68_FROM` [@pa2007]. The Budget gives no decomposition of its lines; demography, GDP or other assumptions could give the same shape, and we draw no inference about the State Pension age it assumes. This is a check, not a finding.

DWP also gives the saving in 2025-26 prices, £`{python} dwp_real`bn; we cannot compare that figure more closely, because the deflator is not published. DWP adds that its savings "`{python} dwp_caution`", and its saving keeps growing, to £`{python} dwp_later`bn in `{python} fy(dwp_later_year)`; our horizon ends in `{python} fy(FINAL)`.

The OBR's estimate of what the triple lock will have added by 2029-30 (@sec-intro) compares the triple lock with earnings uprating since 2011 [@obr_frs2025]. The like-for-like figure on our replay is the triple lock's excess over published earnings since April `{python} first["year"]`, `{python} pct(above_earn, 1)` in `{python} fy(LAST_HIST)`, about `{python} bn(TL_EXCESS_2026, 0)` of basic and new State Pension spending. The adjusted rule started in April `{python} hw_first["first"]` would remove `{python} bn(past_saving["gross"], 1)`, measured against an earnings path that takes CPI in April `{python} susp_year` (@sec-past), so the ratio of the two figures is not the share of the excess that the replay removes.

## Appendix: the two registered models that failed their test {#sec-failed .appendix}

This appendix gives the record of the two registered models of the uprating inputs, both of which failed the test on past forecasts: the baseline model behind the earnings scenarios (@sec-sim-model), the test and its verdict (@sec-test), and the second model, with the distribution its registration requires (@sec-c4).

### The baseline model and the earnings scenarios' paths {#sec-sim-model}

The baseline model (@sec-paths-method) leaves the furlough months of 2020–21 out of its fit. Its coefficients are fixed and its shocks are past pairs of residuals, so prices and earnings keep their joint variation, but the model has no periods of higher or lower volatility and no uncertainty about its coefficients. The simulated months give both the statutory inputs (September CPI, May–July earnings growth) and the calendar-year growth the rest of the model uses. The drift that centres the paths on the OBR's forecast matches calendar-year means only, so the statutory inputs that drive both rules sit off the central path's: over the Aprils `{python} FWD[0]` to `{python} FWD[-1]` the scenarios' mean September CPI is `{python} points(-off_c, 2)` points below the central path's, and their mean May–July earnings growth is `{python} points(-off_e["minus"], 2)` points below it with lower earnings growth and `{python} points(off_e["plus"], 2)` points above it with higher. Because the drift is the smoothest monthly path that meets every calendar-year mean, it also moves the inputs for April `{python} SWITCH` and `{python} SWITCH + 1`; holding both scenarios' earnings inputs for those two Aprils at the lower-earnings scenario's values changes the average $G_t$ in `{python} fy(FINAL)` by at most `{python} points(max(abs(HOLD['G'][k] - SIM_G[k]) for k in SIM_G), 2)` log points. The simulated paths have earnings growth below `{python} FLOOR` in `{python} pct(100 * SIM_BELOW["minus"], 1)` and `{python} pct(100 * SIM_BELOW["plus"], 1)` of those Aprils, and the lead between earnings and CPI changes `{python} num(SIM_SW["minus"], 2)` and `{python} num(SIM_SW["plus"], 2)` times per April transition, against `{python} num(bt_real, 2)` realised in the test on past forecasts (@sec-test). These averages over the sampled paths are rule arithmetic on the stored inputs of the paths run through the microsimulation, weighted as the fiscal figures are; none is a fiscal result.

The fiscal averages for the earnings scenarios are stratified estimates. The model makes `{python} N_POP` equally weighted draws of the baseline model; we sort them into `{python} words(D.N_GROUPS)` groups of equal size by the gap between the rules in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, plus a group in which the rules pay the same, and run `{python} N_DRAWS` of them through the microsimulation, allocated in proportion to each group's size and the spread of that gap within it, with at least two a group. Both earnings scenarios use these groups and the same draws, shifted in opposite directions. Each average's margin is a 95% Monte Carlo interval that combines the sampling of the microsimulation runs with the sampling of the draws; it is conditional on the model and leaves out uncertainty about its coefficients.

### The test on past forecasts {#sec-test}

We registered the test on past OBR forecasts [@obr_hofd2026] before scoring any model; the section of the analysis plan that sets the rule used here is dated `{python} V2["c2_registered"]`. `{python} words(n_forms).capitalize()` versions of the model of prices and earnings enter the test: the baseline model (monthly steps, one lag, resampled residuals) and variants with two lags, annual steps, Student-t shocks and normal shocks. We fit each only on data available before each forecast, centre it on that forecast, and score it with proper scoring rules for each statistic and for the joint outcome [@gneiting2007; @scheuerer2015] and with the coverage of central bands. The scores cover the gap between earnings and CPI in each year, how often the lead changes, how often earnings growth falls below `{python} FLOOR` and the gap the two rules open after four rises. One test uses `{python} words(n_a)` forecasts, one a year from the `{python} D.origins("A")[0]` to the `{python} D.origins("A")[-1]`; another uses `{python} words(n_b)`, from the `{python} D.origins("B")[0]` to the `{python} D.origins("B")[-1]`. @tbl-rule gives the pass rule; we fixed the thresholds together, as a broad screen, before we saw any score. The accuracy condition compares versions with each other, so the baseline model meets it by construction.

The rule changed once, after the first scores and before the second, in two elements. It scores April 2022 as the law applied it (@sec-background), because under the first rule every version failed when we scored April 2022 on the published earnings, which the furlough schemes had distorted. And it no longer lets another version replace a baseline model that fails: only a passing baseline model supplies an average, and otherwise the analysis reports four scenarios. Every threshold in @tbl-rule is as first registered, and we committed the second rule on its own, before we computed any score under it.

With the data available at the October 2026 Budget, the baseline model failed one condition (@tbl-screen). Its error in the share of floor years on the `{python} words(n_a)`-forecast test, an event that sets $d_t > 0$, is `{python} num(fail_value, 3)`, above the limit of `{python} num(fail_limit, 2)`: earnings growth was below the floor in `{python} words(len(FY_BELOW))` of the `{python} words(len(FY_YEARS))` distinct years the windows cover, against about `{python} num(FY_EXP, 1)` that the model's forecasts imply. The test cannot separate `{python} num(fail_value, 3)` from `{python} num(fail_limit, 2)`, and the case for reporting scenarios rests on the direction of the error, which @sec-scen-appendix follows, more than on its margin. All `{python} words(n_forms)` versions share the error, with floor biases from `{python} num(min(fb_all), 3)` to `{python} num(max(fb_all), 3)`; data/results.json holds every version's biases. The OBR forecasts the paths are centred on expected earnings growth to exceed CPI by more than it did, and any such difference between forecast and outturn carries over to the forward paths unchanged. The baseline model passed every other condition, and the rule forbids promoting one of the versions that passed, so it gives no average from these models.

The test has little power. With `{python} words(n_a)` overlapping four-year windows, a model whose bands cover far less than 80% could still pass, and because the upper limit on coverage is `{python} SR['coverage_high']`%, the coverage condition cannot detect bands that are too wide. A pass would also not have been enough. The `{python} words(n_c4)` yearly forecasts with four years of statutory outturns cover `{python} words(len(C4_SPAN))` years of inputs, `{python} C4_SPAN[0]` to `{python} C4_SPAN[-1]`, while the saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` depends on inputs up to `{python} words(C4_AHEAD)` years ahead, and `{python} words(len(C4_SPAN))` years of outturns hold at most `{python} words(len(C4_SPAN) // C4_AHEAD)` independent window of that length. A third rule, the forward rule, applies only to estimates that use OBR forecasts published after this paper's inputs and gives its first verdict in October `{python} C3_REPORT`, after `{python} words(D.C3_YEARS)` years of outcomes. On simulated outcomes a correct model passes its test `{python} pct(100 * D.c3_pass_rate("model is right", 4), 1)` of the time after four years, and a model that states double the true rate of earnings growth below the floor passes `{python} pct(100 * D.c3_pass_rate("true floor rate is 1/2 of the model's", 4), 1)`, so four years of outcomes cannot tell the two apart.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rule
#| tbl-cap: "The pass rule for the test on past forecasts, April 2022 scored as the law applied it. A version passes only if it meets every condition on both tests."
rule = [
    ["Coverage", f"Between {SR['coverage_low']}% and {SR['coverage_high']}% of outcomes, yearly and after four years, fall inside the central 80% band"],
    ["Coverage, plausible range", f"The range of plausible coverage after four years includes {SR['wilson_contains']}%"],
    ["Bias in the yearly gap", f"Average error in earnings minus CPI at most {SR['gap_bias']} points"],
    ["Bias in lead changes", f"Average error in the number of lead changes at most {SR['switch_bias']} a forecast"],
    ["Bias in floor years", f"Average error in the share of years with earnings growth below {FLOOR} at most {SR['floor_bias']}"],
    ["Accuracy scores", f"No score more than {pct(100 * (SR['score_ratio'] - 1), 0)} worse than the baseline model's"],
    ["Past years", f"The realised gap since 2011 between the {ordinal(SR['past_low'])} and {ordinal(SR['past_high'])} percentiles of its paths"],
]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Condition", "Threshold"], rule, "ll")))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-screen
#| tbl-cap: "The test on past forecasts, April 2022 scored as in law: coverage, accuracy and verdict. Seven forecasts: March 2016 to March 2022; thirteen: June 2010 to March 2022. Plausible range: the 95% Wilson interval for four-year coverage, which must include 80%. Score ratio: the largest ratio to the baseline model's scores."
SCORES = ("gap_crps", "switch_crps", "floor_crps", "energy", "variogram")
sc_all = D.C2["scores"]
body = []
for form, verdict in forms.items():
    cells = []
    for test in ("A", "B"):
        r = sc_all[test]["suspended"][form]
        cells += [pct(100 * r["annual_gap_coverage"]["mean"], 0), f'{r["terminal_coverage"]["hits"]} of {r["terminal_scored_origins"]}']
    lo_w, hi_w = sc_all["A"]["suspended"][form]["terminal_coverage"]["wilson95_independent"]
    worst = max(sc_all[t]["suspended"][form][k]["mean"] / sc_all[t]["suspended"][D.PRIMARY_FORM][k]["mean"]
                for t in ("A", "B") for k in SCORES)
    body.append([D.FORM_NAMES.get(form, form), *cells, f"{pct(100 * lo_w, 0)} to {pct(100 * hi_w, 0)}",
                 num(worst, 2), "Pass" if verdict["passes"] else "Fail"])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Version", "Seven forecasts: Yearly", "Seven forecasts: Four-year",
                           "Thirteen forecasts: Yearly", "Thirteen forecasts: Four-year", "Plausible range",
                           "Score ratio", "Verdict"], body, "lrrrrrrl")))
```

### The second model {#sec-c4}

```{python}
RES, DR, DC = D.C4_RES, D.C4_DRIFT, D.C4_DECOMP
c4_first_april = DR["determination_years"][0] + 1  # each determination year's inputs set the next April's rise
c4_last_april = DR["determination_years"][-1] + 1
top = RES["tails_of_share_2039"]["highest_5pct"]
bottom = RES["tails_of_share_2039"]["lowest_5pct"]
late = RES["late_target_years"]
late_w = DR["weight_on_late_targets_from_year_5"]
first_drift = next(i for i, v in enumerate(DR["mean_error_exact"]["cpi"]) if v != 0)  # year five
drift_april = DR["determination_years"][first_drift] + 1
ex_c, ex_e = DR["mean_error_exact"]["cpi"], DR["mean_error_exact"]["earnings"]
e_peak = max(range(len(ex_e)), key=lambda i: ex_e[i])
GAPS = DC["gap_to_scenarios_2039"]
sd_c4 = {v: (min(DC["input_sd_points"][v]), max(DC["input_sd_points"][v])) for v in ("cpi", "earnings")}
sd_sc = {v: (min(min(DC["scenarios"][k]["input_sd_points"][v]) for k in ("minus", "plus")),
             max(max(DC["scenarios"][k]["input_sd_points"][v]) for k in ("minus", "plus"))) for v in ("cpi", "earnings")}
c4_sens = D.c4_sensitivities_passing()
assert c4_sens == ["no_centre_uncertainty"]
c4_none_2034 = D.c4_distribution(D.C4_YEARS[0])["p25"] == 0
# The other registered sensitivities, which would have failed: their failed checks, from scores.json.
CHR, LOO, RAW = (D.c4_sensitivity_failures(k) for k in ("chronological", "leave_one_forecast_out", "raw_errors"))
chr_a = D.c4_sensitivity_summary("chronological")["terminal_coverage"]  # registered on the seven-forecast test only
assert [c for t, c, _ in CHR if t == "A"] == ["terminal_coverage", "terminal Wilson band contains 0.80"]
loo_fb = next(float(v) for t, c, v in LOO if (t, c) == ("A", "|floor_bias|"))
loo_rest = [(t, c, v) for t, c, v in LOO if (t, c) != ("A", "|floor_bias|")]
assert [(t, c) for t, c, _ in loo_rest] == [("A", "switch_crps ratio to the first model"),
                                            ("B", "four-year gaps inside the central-50% band (added)")]
raw_fb = next(float(v) for t, c, v in RAW if (t, c) == ("A", "|floor_bias|"))
```

After the baseline model failed, we registered a second model of the inputs before scoring it, together with what the paper would report if it failed: scenarios only, every score, and the model's distribution of the share of spending saved once, in an appendix. The analysis plan holds the registration in a dated section, pushed before the model's code and its scores (@tbl-timeline). The registration states its own limits: its hold-out is not chronological, we designed the model after seeing every earlier score and the whole record of forecast errors, and it is the `{python} C4_NTH` version of the model scored against these forecasts. The second model centres each path on the OBR's forecast and takes its errors from the OBR's own record: the errors of the `{python} words(n_c4)` forecasts, one a year, from the `{python} D.origins("B")[0]` to the `{python} D.origins("B")[-1]`, one to four years ahead. Each path takes one past forecast's errors for its first four years, continues with the four-year-ahead errors of the target years that followed, and adds a draw of the uncertainty in the average error.

It faced the same test as the baseline model, with three added checks on its central bands, and met every scored condition but one (@tbl-c4-scores); the past-years check could not be scored, because no record of forecast errors exists before 2011, and does not count as met. On the thirteen-forecast test its variogram score, a proper score of how the yearly gaps move together [@scheuerer2015], is `{python} num(c4_value, 3)` times the baseline model's, above the limit of `{python} num(c4_limit, 2)`. Across `{python} count(C4S["n_seed_sets"])` other sets of random seeds, computed after the verdict, outside the registration, the ratio runs from `{python} num(C4S["variogram_ratio_b"]["min"], 3)` to `{python} num(C4S["variogram_ratio_b"]["max"], 3)`, so the failure does not depend on the seeds. It does depend on single forecasts: leaving any one forecast's score out of both models' averages, also computed after the verdict, puts the ratio between `{python} num(C4_D1["min"], 3)` and `{python} num(C4_D1["max"], 3)`, so the test cannot separate the score from its limit. On the seven-forecast test its floor bias, `{python} num(C4_FB, 3)`, sits below the limit of `{python} num(C4_FB_LIM, 2)`, but across the same seed sets it runs from `{python} num(C4S["floor_bias_a"]["min"], 3)` to `{python} num(C4S["floor_bias_a"]["max"], 3)` and exceeds the limit in `{python} words(C4S["floor_bias_a"]["sets_above_limit"])` of them. Of the sensitivities the registration named, which do not enter the verdict, only the model without the draw of the average error and without the small-sample correction would have met every check, and the rule forbids promoting it.

The analysis plan requires what follows because the second model failed its test. Every figure in @tbl-c4-dist is the output of a model that failed its registered test and is not a probability statement: the paper attaches no likelihood to any of them, takes none as an estimate and converts none to cash. Years five to twelve of each path are untested, because no forecast in the record runs that far. The model draws `{python} count(D.C4_PATHS)` paths of September CPI and May–July earnings growth around the OBR central path, for the Aprils `{python} c4_first_april` to `{python} c4_last_april`, and applies both rules to each path in rule arithmetic.`{python} " In " + fy(D.C4_YEARS[0]) + " the lower quartile is zero: on those paths no price- or floor-led April from the switch has yet been followed by an earnings-led one." if c4_none_2034 else ""` The paths hold only `{python} count(RES["distinct_histories"])` distinct histories of past errors, so the quartiles and tails rest on few past years; the outer percentiles and threshold shares that the registration also named are in `{python} (D.C4_DIR / 'rule_arithmetic.json').relative_to(D.ROOT)`. From year five the model's centre drifts above the OBR path, because later years draw the four-year-ahead errors for `{python} late[0]` to `{python} late[-1]`, which are positive, more often than uniform sampling would, and its inputs vary more than the baseline model's; both raise the share saved. We computed the seed sets, the single-score drops, the counts of histories and the drift after the verdict; none of them was registered, and none is the result of a corrected model.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-c4-dist

for y in D.C4_YEARS:
    for what, label in (("share", "share of spending (%)"), ("G", "G (log points)")):
        d = D.c4_distribution(y, what)
```

## Appendix: the Bayesian forecast's checks {#sec-b1-appendix .appendix}

This appendix gives the record of the model's registration and of its convergence gate, the posterior predictive checks (@tbl-b1-ppc), the scores under two hold-outs and every sensitivity run (@tbl-b1-sens, @tbl-b1-sens-later).

The second model's registration said that another model would need another registration that counts the failures (@sec-b1-method). The specification of the Bayesian forecast is that registration. The analysis plan's commit that holds it, with the priors, the checks and how the paper reports them, precedes the model's first code and its first fit in the public record (@tbl-timeline), which shows that order and no more.

The gate requires, for every parameter, a rank-normalised split $\widehat{R}$ of at most `{python} num(BF['convergence']['gate']['rhat_max'], 2)` and bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least `{python} count(BF['convergence']['gate']['ess_min'])`, and at most `{python} words(BF['convergence']['gate']['divergences_max'])` divergent transitions in the fit. Every chain starts from the same point, near the prior means, which weakens $\widehat{R}$ as a check. As first coded, the bound on $\Phi$ was a wall of zero density inside the sampler, which tripped the divergence diagnostic in the first fit and in the registered rerun: the first fit had `{python} words(D.B1_WALL_DIV[0])` divergent transitions and the rerun, at a higher target acceptance, `{python} words(D.B1_WALL_DIV[1])`. The plan lets a coding error be fixed in a commit that says so, and we read the wall as such an error; its sentence on the gate makes no exception for one, so the fit as first coded did not meet the gate as written (@sec-b1-method). Sampling without the wall and then discarding the `{python} words(BRB["draws_outside"])` draws outside the bound, which is rejection sampling, targets the same truncated posterior; it gives `{python} words(BW["divergences"]) if BW["divergences"] else "no"` divergent transitions, $\widehat{R}$ at most `{python} num(BW["rhat"], 4)` and effective sample sizes of at least `{python} count(math.floor(min(BW["ess_bulk"], BW["ess_tail"])))`. The wall-coded draws give the same median saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, `{python} bn(B1_GATE_WALL, 2)` against `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 2)`. The commit that makes that change precedes the first forecast figure in the public record.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-timeline
#| tbl-cap: "The public record of each specification: when we pushed it, and the minutes to the first code and first results (GitHub, UTC). It shows only that each specification was public before its code and results."
def _after(a, b):
    s = round((datetime.fromisoformat(b.replace("Z", "+00:00")) - datetime.fromisoformat(a.replace("Z", "+00:00"))).total_seconds())
    return f"{s} seconds" if s < 120 else f"{round(s / 60)} minutes"
def _when(a):
    d = datetime.fromisoformat(a.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    return f"{d.day} {d.strftime('%B %Y, %H:%M')}"
TL_ROWS = [("The second model (registration)", V2["c4_pushed"], "registration", "code", "scores"),
           ("Results under stated volatility (specification, not a registration)", V2["v1_pushed"], "spec", "code", "figures"),
           ("The Bayesian forecast (specification with no pass rule)", V2["b1_pushed"], "spec", "code", "fit")]
body = [[label, _when(d[a]), _after(d[a], d[b]), _after(d[a], d[c])] for label, d, a, b, c in TL_ROWS]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Specification", "Pushed", "First code, after", "First results, after"], body, "llrr")))
```

In `{python} count(D.B1_VAL["replicated_error_records"]["replications"])` replications of the error record (@tbl-b1-ppc), the registered statistics closest to the edge of the central `{python} pct(D.B1_PPC_BAND, 0)` of replications are the changes of lead between earnings and CPI per four-year window, `{python} num(B1_SW[0], 2)` realised against a replicated median of `{python} num(B1_SW[1], 2)`, and the standard deviation of one-year-ahead CPI errors, `{python} num(B1_SDC1[0], 2)` points against `{python} num(B1_SDC1[1], 2)`. A check we added after seeing these, on the spread of the earnings error less the CPI error, finds the realised spread inside the replications at every horizon.

We refit the model `{python} words(B1_HOLD)` times under each of two hold-outs, once for each forecast of the test in @sec-test without the data that forecast's hold-out forbids. Under a chronological hold-out, which uses only errors observed before each forecast, the floor bias on the `{python} words(n_a)`-forecast test runs from `{python} num(B1_SEEDS_CH[0], 4)` to `{python} num(B1_SEEDS_CH[1], 4)` across `{python} words(B1_SEEDS_CH[2])` sets of path seeds, and `{python} words(B1_SEEDS_CH[2] - B1_SEEDS_CH[3])` of them `{python} 'misses' if B1_SEEDS_CH[2] - B1_SEEDS_CH[3] == 1 else 'miss'` the limit of `{python} num(FB_LIM, 2)`; under the second model's hold-out, which drops every forecast sharing a target year, it runs from `{python} num(B1_SEEDS_TY[0], 4)` to `{python} num(B1_SEEDS_TY[1], 4)` and every set misses. Every other limit is met under both. The variogram score, on which the second model failed at `{python} num(c4_value, 3)` times the baseline model's, is `{python} num(min(B1_VG), 2)` to `{python} num(max(B1_VG), 2)` times it.

Each run in @tbl-b1-sens and @tbl-b1-sens-later changes one thing, except the persistent-volatility run, and every refit met the convergence gate. The analysis plan registered the first group before any forecast figure existed and the second after an internal review, before running it; we added the statutory-basis fit on the calendar-basis cells after seeing the calendar-basis fit. None replaces the headline.

```{python}
T1, T2, T3 = D.B1_APP["t1"], D.B1_APP["t2"], D.B1_APP["t3"]
T1W, T3W = T1["convergence"]["worst"], T3["convergence"]["worst"]
T2R = T2["runs"]
T2_SHIFT = max(v["mean_shift_points"]["max_over_years"][k] for v in T2R.values() for k in ("cpi", "earnings"))
T2_NEG = [T2R[k]["share_path_years_below_zero"]["cpi"] for k in ("record_minimum_median_centred", "record_minimum_mean_centred")]
T2_FLOOR = [v["earnings_below_floor_share"] for v in T2R.values()]
T2_L = pct(T2R["record_minimum_median_centred"]["bound_points"], 1)
T4 = D.B1_APP["t4"]
T4R = T4["runs"]
assert D.b1_tilt("c2_test_windows") < D.b1_tilt("years_2001_2025") < B1G["p50"]
T3_MULT = T3["posterior"]["sd_multiplier_median_by_year"]
T3_PEAK = max(T3_MULT, key=T3_MULT.get)
assert T3["convergence"]["gate_met_as_written"] and not T3["settings"]["rerun"] and T1W["divergences"] == 0
assert all(T2R[k]["share_path_years_below_zero"]["cpi"] == 0 for k in ("zero_median_centred", "zero_mean_centred"))
assert abs(D.b1_app("t1", stat="p95") - B1G["p95"]) < 0.1 and abs(D.b1_app("t3", stat="p95") - B1G["p95"]) < 0.1
assert max(D.b1_app(k) for k in T2R) < D.b1_sup("c") - 0.5 < B1G["p50"]  # the prose: lower than run (c)
```

We specified four further runs on 14 November 2026, after seeing every result above, and pushed each specification before its code. The first refits the model with the bound on $\Phi$ imposed by a smooth change of variables, with its Jacobian in the density, so the sampler meets no wall. Its posterior agrees with the headline's draws: no reported percentile of any parameter differs by more than `{python} num(T1["posterior_check"]["max_abs_quantile_gap_in_sd"], 2)` of a posterior standard deviation. It meets the gate's limits on its first run, with `{python} words(T1W["divergences"]) if T1W["divergences"] else "no"` divergent transitions, $\widehat{R}$ at most `{python} num(T1W["rhat"], 4)` and effective sample sizes of at least `{python} count(math.floor(min(T1W["ess_bulk"], T1W["ess_tail"])))`, and gives a median of `{python} bn(D.b1_app("t1"), 2)` against `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 2)`, with a Monte Carlo error of `{python} bn(T1["monte_carlo_se"][str(FINAL)]["gross_p50"], 2)`. The divergences thus came from how we first coded the bound, not from the posterior; the record that the fit as first coded exceeded the gate's limit stands.

The second run keeps the fit and compresses the lower side of each forward input towards a bound it never passes: an input with centre $f$, deviation $\varepsilon < 0$ and bound $L$ becomes $L + (f - L)\exp(\varepsilon / (f - L))$. The bound is zero or `{python} T2_L`, just below the lowest statutory input since 1989. The compression raises each input's mean, by up to `{python} num(T2_SHIFT, 1)` points, so @tbl-b1-sens-later also gives each bound with the paths re-centred on the OBR central path. These runs lower the median by more than setting negative inputs to zero does, because they shrink every shortfall below the centre, and with it the floor's lead over low earnings growth; they transform the forward paths and are not a model with skewed shocks fitted to the record. The third run replaces the Student-t shock with a normal shock whose log variance follows a first-order autoregression over 1990 to 2026, fitted to both records and continued forward. It met the gate on its first run, puts the posterior median of the persistence of the log variance at `{python} num(T3["posterior"]["phi_h"]["p50"], 2)`, lowers the median to `{python} bn(D.b1_app("t3"), 1)` and leaves the `{python} V1_HI` percentile where the headline has it.

The fourth run, a diagnostic of the floor years, reweights the forecast's own paths by exponential tilting, as @sec-scen-appendix does for the scenarios, so that the share of years with earnings growth below `{python} FLOOR` falls from `{python} pct(100 * T4["unweighted_floor_share"], 0)` to the `{python} pct(100 * T4R["years_2001_2025"]["target_floor_share"], 0)` of 2001–2025 or to the `{python} pct(100 * T4R["c2_test_windows"]["target_floor_share"], 1)` realised in the test's windows; the median falls to `{python} bn(D.b1_tilt("years_2001_2025"), 1)` and `{python} bn(D.b1_tilt("c2_test_windows"), 1)`. The tilt also raises the paths' mean earnings growth, so the run shows only the direction and rough size of the forecast's dependence on floor years.
